Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, thank you for the opportunity to provide information neither for nor against LD 1389, An Act to Create the Building Opportunity Through Out-of-school Time Program.

This bill would create a new chapter of Title 22 that would establish a competitive grant program to expand out-of-school time programming for school-age-youth. This includes enhancing current programs, reducing barriers to participation, and other activities to improve access to these programs. The bill would appropriate $5 million in General Fund for this purpose and require OCFS to begin issuing grants by 12/1/26 to nonprofits and libraries. LD 1389 would also require monitoring of and reporting on this grant program by OCFS.

OCFS greatly appreciates the desire to increase programming opportunities for out-of-school time programs, but we are concerned with the significant fiscal allocation proposed in this bill. OCFS already supports care and programming for school-age children and youth through the Child Care Affordability Program (CCAP) and the Integrating Outcomes for Youth (IOY) program. The CCAP rules permit families to receive an award of up to 50 hours of care per week for a school-age youth and allow recreational programs to participate in CCAP as license-exempt providers. IOY promotes health, safety, and resilience; and provides connections to workforce and educational opportunities for Maine youth through OCFS contracts with Boys and Girls Clubs and other community-based organizations.

Ensuring the accessibility of out-of-school time programming for families is an important goal and has been a driving force behind efforts over the last few years to ensure that CCAP could be used to pay for care in recreational programs. The majority of CCAP funding comes from the federal government through the Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG), this allows Maine to support out-of-school time care for youth in a manner not wholly dependent on State General Fund.

OCFS appreciates the Committee's ongoing support of the CCAP program as we seek to create an array of opportunities that address the wide variety of needs among Maine youth and families.
Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions during your deliberation of this bill.
Sincerely,
Bobbi L. Johnson, LMSW Director Office of Child and Family Services Maine Department of Health and Human Services

to the Health and Human Services Committee Tuesday, April 8, 2025, 1 p.m.
By Jason Judd, Executive Director Educate Maine
Chairs Ingwersen and Meyer, distinguished members of the Health and Human Services Committee, I am Jason Judd, Executive Director of Educate Maine and I appear before you today in support of LD 1389, An Act to Create the Building Opportunity Through Out-of-School Time (BOOST) Program.
Educate Maine is a business-led education organization which champions career readiness and education attainment of Maine people by supporting education along the full continuum of life - from early childhood through adulthood. We also offer research and Maine-specific data to help inform your decisions on key education issues.
As a business-led organization, I will focus my remarks and our support on how this proposal before you today will support Maine's workforce and our economy.
First, we start with the knowledge that, according to data in the newest Maine Kids Count Data Book, 69.6 percent of all Maine children under the age of six have all parents in the workforce. As you have heard me say before in this committee, for our youngest children that underscores the need for full-day, safe, reliable and affordable child care while parents work. But those needs don't stop once a child turns five years old and starts formal school. Working parents need care for their children, up to age 13, for the hours they are working and for which their child/children are not in school. Given the rural nature of Maine, and the fact that so many working parents commute to jobs outside the communities they live in, often that means that parents need child care for 10 or more hours a day. That is at least three additional hours beyond the typical school day.
That's why out-of-school care, also known as before and after school care, is so important. And similar to child care for Maine's youngest children, Maine lacks an adequate supply of this care.

According to data from the National Afterschool Alliance, we know that for every Maine child enrolled in an after school program, there are five additional children, and their parents, waiting for such an opportunity.
Out-of-school programs in Maine - before school, after school, vacation camps and summer day programs -- consistently have waitlist. Capacity is simply not meeting need.
As a result, more parents are leaving the workforce, reducing their work hours, or being forced to move to less desirable jobs. That hurts their families economically and has a negative impact on the productivity of the businesses/non-profits they work for, and our local and state economies.
At the same time, we know from research that the academic enrichment offered in out-of-school time programs - like help with homework, extra reading and reading supports, and exposure to activities in STEM subjects, improve student engagement and learning. It also helps support increase student attendance at school, reduces risky behaviors and increases health and wellness outcomes. All of these foundational pieces work together to increase high school graduation rates and raises student aspirations to participate in post-secondary and careers opportunities.
The $5 million investment sought in LD 1389 will not reduce all of the out-of-school programs' waitlists, but it is a critical start.
I urge your unanimous support of LD 1389.

Good afternoon, Senator Ingwersen and Representative Meyer, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, my name is Rita Furlow. The Maine Children's Alliance is a statewide non-partisan, non-profit research and advocacy organization whose mission is to promote sound public policies to improve the lives of children, youth, and families in Maine.
At the Children's Alliance, we believe that Maine's future prosperity depends upon how our children are doing today. We know that 70 percent of children under the age of six have both parents in the workforce.1 While the need for child care for our youngest children in Maine is often discussed, we know that the child care needs for parents do not end when children arrive at school - they simply change. Depending upon their work schedules, many working parents still require child care either before or after the school day.
Over the past few years, you've likely heard about the shortage of child care, especially for our youngest children. However, finding care for children for just one or two hours a day can be even more challenging for families. Not surprisingly, most child care providers are filling any open slots with families that need care for the full day. While some schools may receive a federal grant from the 21st Century Community Learning Center ($2.5 million in funding available for FY 25-26) or private funding, these grants do not meet the need across the state for before and after school programs. According to the National Afterschool Alliance, in Maine, for every one child enrolled in an afterschool program, there are five more children waiting for care.
LD 1359 would provide $5 million in funding to support afterschool programming and would require the Office of Child and Family Services to create rules to implement the Building Opportunity Through Out-of-school Time Program to support the needs of children and families. Non-profit organizations could apply for grants through a competitive grant process to support programing for school-age children, with program grant awards issued by December 1, 2026.
